title: People who changed rights
log: 2026-11-01T08:04:33Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new
2026-11-01T08:14:05Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

match.reason: The closest bank point, The development of human rights, covers the historical growth of rights through documents and campaigns, while this point asks how individuals and groups use cases, campaigns and protest to push governments and courts to protect rights better, which is a different idea.

draft.title: People who changed rights
card: Rights are not only set by governments. Individuals and groups have pushed parliaments and courts to protect rights better.
a person takes a dispute to court. A ruling can change how a right is understood and applied. Eddie Mabo's case led the High Court in 1992 to recognise native title.

a group organises over time to win public support and press for law change. The 1967 referendum campaign led to a vote that changed the Constitution so that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people were counted in the census.
people take public action, such as marches and rallies, to show strong support for change and draw attention to a right.
draft.remember: Change in rights can come from people acting, not only from governments.

a.q: Eddie Mabo took a dispute about land to the High Court, and the Court recognised native title in 1992. Which method of change does this show?
opts: A case that changed how a right is applied
A campaign run to win a public vote
A protest march to draw public attention
A law passed by parliament without any court
a.why: Mabo used a court case, and the High Court's ruling changed how land rights were recognised. It is not a protest, because the change came from a court ruling rather than from public action to draw attention.

b.q: A group in a town spends years gathering signatures, speaking to the media and meeting MPs until parliament passes a law protecting a right. What method is this mainly?
opts: A campaign to win support and press for law change
A case where a court rules on a dispute
A protest limited to one rally for attention
A referendum that the group itself held
b.why: The group organised over time to win public support and press for a new law, which is a campaign. It is not a case, because no court ruling was involved. It is not a single protest, because the effort was sustained over years.
b.clue: Look at how long the group worked and who it aimed to persuade.

a.best: A case that changed how a right is applied

b.best: A campaign to win support and press for law change

problems.detail: The 1967 referendum line is a simplification. The change removed s127, which excluded Aboriginal people from official population counts. The vote also gave the Commonwealth power to make laws for Aboriginal people, often seen as the more significant change. 'Counted in the census' alone is imprecise and close to a common misconception. Better: 'counted in official population figures and brought under Commonwealth law-making power'.

The right option is the longest and repeats the card's definition of a campaign almost word for word ('win public support and press for law change'). A student could match the wording without understanding the idea.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer and the Mabo facts are correct. The card's 1967 referendum line oversimplifies what changed, and question b's right option stands out by length and by echoing the card's wording.
